subtype: Gradual demands on time and loyalty [Receiver]
passage:
Looking back, I can't point to the day it changed. That's the scary part.
In first year Abhinav and I both went to the "leadership circle" on Tuesday evenings. Free chai, big talk about purpose. It was good.
Then it was Tuesdays and Thursdays. Then weekends, "for serious members". Then a "contribution" of a thousand rupees for the Level Two teachings, the ones outsiders "weren't ready for". Then: "Keep your distance from people who drain your energy." Abhinav had started asking questions. So I stopped replying to him.
Each step felt tiny. I only saw the whole thing in March, when I tried to write down how I'd spent the week for a time-management task. Twenty-two hours. Four thousand rupees since October. Almost no old friends.
I sat there staring at the page. Then I called Abhinav. He picked up on the first ring and said, "Took you long enough," and I laughed so hard I nearly cried.
Ujjwal

qa.q: How many hours in the week did Ujjwal count for the circle?
How did Ujjwal feel on seeing the week written down?
qa.a: Ujjwal was shocked and shaken, sitting and staring at the page, because each step had felt tiny and the total had been invisible from inside.

qa.q: What turning point helped Ujjwal see the change?
qa.a: Writing down the week for a time-management task showed the hours, the money and the lost friends in one place, which led Ujjwal to call Abhinav.

qa.q: What was it like for Abhinav when Ujjwal stopped replying?
qa.a: Abhinav was cut off for asking questions, yet stayed ready to help, which shows in how quickly he picked up and joked, "Took you long enough".

grounding: Over months a student is asked for more time, money and distance from doubters by a group offering special teachings, and only sees the total change later.

passage:
Counselling note, Student Wellness Centre. Written by Simran, counsellor, 12 November.
Tanvir, second-year engineering, came in on his own today. He spoke quietly and kept checking his phone. He described joining a "self-mastery" group in February: one weekly session at first, then three, then weekend camps. Since August he has paid for "advanced modules", and was told recently that his roommates were "negative influences" and he should not discuss the group with them or his family.
What I observed: he could not say when things had changed. "Every step made sense at the time," he said twice.
We drew a timeline together on paper, month by month. When he saw it, he went very still.
Next steps: with his agreement, I called his mother while he was in the room and she will visit this weekend. I have booked him for Friday. He agreed to skip this weekend's camp and to keep talking to his roommates.

qa.q: When did Tanvir join the self-mastery group?
What does Tanvir's repeated line "Every step made sense at the time" suggest he feels?
qa.a: It suggests Tanvir feels confused and a little ashamed, unable to see how he got so deep because each demand seemed small on its own.

qa.q: Why was drawing the timeline a useful step?
qa.a: Laying out the months on paper let Tanvir see the whole change at once, which the small steps had hidden, so he could decide from outside the group's view.

qa.q: How might Tanvir's roommates have experienced the months he was told they were "negative influences"?
qa.a: They may have felt pushed away without knowing why, and his renewed openness gives them a chance to reconnect.

grounding: A counsellor records a student who, over months, was drawn into more hours, payments, secrecy and distance from others, and helps him see the whole pattern.
